# Results — Study 459 (Hikkake pattern, the false-breakout trap)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **the
hikkake trap forecasts a reversal: an inside bar, a false breakout one way, then a snap-back
through the range, so you trade the reversal direction** — encoded as a mechanical rule. An
inside bar is ``high_i < high_{i-1}`` and ``low_i > low_{i-1}``; within a 3-bar window a close
must poke beyond the inside-bar range and then snap back through it (long after a failed
downside break, short after a failed upside break). Entry is the **next close** (one documented
lag), and we measure the direction-signed forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **1 438** mechanical hikkake traps pooled across the 5 tapes (window = 3): **548 long / 890 short** |
| Timing / costs | trap confirmed on the snap-back close; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per trade |

> **Direction-signed.** Returns are signed by the trade direction (long after a failed
> downside break, short after a failed upside break). The random baseline is matched not only
> on instrument/epoch/hold but on the same **long/short mix**, so it carries the same net
> exposure to the tape's drift — the only honest control for a mixed-direction signal.

## The signal — hikkake vs a drift/exposure-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number on a drifting tape; the **Welch hikkake-vs-random**
*t* is the test that matters. Δ = hikkake − random.

| horizon | n | hikkake | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (hik−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 1437 | −5.5 bps  | 49% | −0.84 | −2.1 bps  | **−3.4 bps**  | −7.5 bps  | −0.35 | 0.729 |
| 10-day | 1435 | −16.7 bps | 49% | −1.89 | −3.7 bps  | **−13.1 bps** | −18.7 bps | −0.98 | 0.326 |
| 20-day | 1433 | −34.4 bps | 48% | −2.57 | −12.4 bps | **−22.0 bps** | −36.4 bps | −1.18 | 0.237 |
| 60-day | 1423 | −94.0 bps | 46% | −4.10 | −21.3 bps | **−72.7 bps** | −96.0 bps | −2.23 | 0.026 |

Read it carefully. The hikkake's signed return is **negative at every horizon** and *worse than
the random baseline at every horizon* (Δ = −3.4 / −13.1 / −22.0 / −72.7 bps). The signal does
not forecast the reversal it claims; if anything the short-heavy mix is fighting the tape's
upward drift, so the rule **loses to its own exposure-matched random control** — significantly
so at 60 days (Welch *t* = −2.23, *p* = 0.026, in the *wrong* direction for the believers). The
hikkake-vs-random Welch *t* is **never positive past noise** — it never clears the desk's
*t* ≥ 2 bar in favour of the rule. The trap does not forecast.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — negative deltas almost everywhere

| ticker | entries | hikkake | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (hik−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 282 | −53.8 bps | −1.97 | −22.2 bps | **−31.6 bps** |
| QQQ | 297 | −25.3 bps | −0.78 | −16.3 bps | **−9.0 bps** |
| IWM | 288 | −36.3 bps | −1.21 | −22.7 bps | **−13.5 bps** |
| DIA | 287 | −21.9 bps | −1.01 | −33.0 bps | **+11.1 bps** |
| GLD | 284 | −35.4 bps | −0.99 | +32.8 bps | **−68.1 bps** |

Only **DIA** edges out a positive delta (+11.1 bps, noise); in 4 of 5 names the famous trap
*underperforms* an exposure-matched random entry. No coherent cross-sectional edge — the
hallmark of a rule with nothing under the hood.

## Direction placebo — scramble which way the trap forecasts, nothing changes

The decisive "does the trap's *direction* matter?" test: keep every hikkake **date** and the
same trade count, but randomly flip each trade's **direction**, destroying the trap's defining
geometry (which way it predicts) while keeping the entry marginal. If the trap genuinely
forecast the reversal, randomly flipping direction would collapse the result.

| test | observed signed 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-direction hikkake | −53.8 bps | **0.978** | 500 |

**98% of direction-scrambled hikkakes match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.978) — i.e. the
real, "correctly" directed trap is among the *worst* of all coin-flip directions. The hikkake's
defining content — *which way it forecasts* — carries no information. "The trap forecasts the
reversal" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real trap

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* hikkake-reversal (knob `edge`), the same rule behaves
exactly as it must — so the flat/negative real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not a
dead detector.

| planted edge | n | hikkake | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no trap) | 451 | −33.0 bps | 47% | −1.42 |
| **0.50** (real planted reversal) | 366 | +963.5 bps | 72% | **+8.89** |

With no planted reversal the control stays below the bar (*t* = −1.42 — no false positive); a
real planted trap lights up at *t* = +8.89 with a 72% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The direction-signed hikkake does **not** beat a drift/exposure-matched
  random baseline at any horizon (Δ = −3.4 / −13.1 / −22.0 / −72.7 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the
  hikkake-vs-random Welch *t* is never positive past noise, and is significantly *negative* at
  60 days, *t* = −2.23). The negative one-sample *t*'s are the short-heavy mix paying the
  inverse of the index drift, not a forecast.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no edge to capture — the signed return is negative gross
  and net, and costs only deepen the hole. Nothing to scale.
- **"Does the false-breakout trap forecast?" — BUSTED.** The scrambled-direction placebo leaves
  the result intact (*p* = 0.978): randomly flipping which way each trap "predicts" does at
  least as well as the real direction 98% of the time, so the trap's defining geometry carries
  no forecasting information. The hikkake is a *post-hoc* chart label, not a forecasting pattern.
